newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-S&P affirms Queensland AAA/A1+, AA-A1+.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-S&P affirms Queensland AAA/A1+, AA-A1+.

text.p: Standard and Poor's Corp said on Thursday it had affirmed its AAA long term and A1+ short term domestic ratings for the government and entities of the Australian state of Queensland.
S&P also said it had affirmed its AA long term and A1+ short term ratings on foreign currency borrowings.
The ratings also apply to Queensland Treasury Corp.
The foreign currency ratings reflect the sovereign credit risks associated with the AA rating of the Commonwealth Government of Australia, the ratings agency said.

"The local currency ratings of the Government of Queensland reflect its very low debt levels, its continued financial strength and flexibility, and the positive outlook for the state's economy," S&P said.
S&P said the net debt burden of the Queensland total state sector is the lowest among Australian states and territories.
S&P said this gave the state flexibility to increase state debt levels without placing undue pressure on the state budget.

"Queensland's low debt history is a result of successive state governments taking a conservative fiscal stance, which included funding superannuation obligations as they occurred and financing social infrastructure investment solely through recurrent revenues and not through borrowings," it said.
S&P said the outlook was stable.

"Latest information indicates that the total state sector is continuing to maintain a strong financial position in fiscal 1997, with a significant negative net borrowing requirement expected," it said.

S&P said that while Queensland's economic growth in fiscal 1996 was more than one percentage point below the growth rate for the rest of Australia, the state's economic growth was expected to be moderate to strong over the medium term as a result of expanding tourism and mining.

With net debt declining in fiscal 1996 as a result of negative net borrowing requirements of the general government sector, net debt to gross state product (GSP) declined to 7.8 percent from 8.7 percent in fiscal 1995 and net debt to budgetary revenue fell to 26.7 percent from 30.4 percent.
The state's debt servicing ratio was low, with net interest paid to operating revenue ratio currently at 1.5 percent, S&P said.
"Queensland's strong financial position was maintained in fiscal 1996 despite a fall in the total state sector's operating surplus," it said.

"Combined with a less protected manufacturing sector, more favourable labour market conditions and a further diversification of the Queensland economy, these factors shold lead to real GSP rates of about one percentage point above the national average in the medium term," S&P said.

"Nevertheless, the Queensland economy has the potential to be subject to economic swings larger than the national average because of the significance of the cyclically sensitive commodity sector," the ratings agency said.
